steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Odysseus's wanderings take him through a series of increasingly dangerous encounters with monsters and divine beings

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Lotus-Eaters offer a fruit that causes forgetfulness — they represent the temptation of abandoning the journey

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Cyclops Polyphemus represents uncivilised brutality — he eats men raw and ignores xenia and the gods

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Circe transforms Odysseus's men into pigs — she represents the dangers of female seduction and enchantment

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What do the Lotus-Eaters symbolise in the Odyssey? | Q: Why must Odysseus choose between Scylla and Charybdis? | Q: How does Circe differ from Calypso as a threat?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: They represent the temptation of forgetting — abandoning the struggle of life and the journey home for passive comfort and oblivion. Those who eat the lotus lose all desire to return. | They are positioned on opposite sides of a narrow strait. Avoiding Charybdis (the whirlpool that destroys the whole ship) means sailing close to Scylla (who takes six men). There is no safe path — onl | Circe is an active danger who transforms men into animals; Calypso is a passive temptation who offers comfort and immortality. Circe threatens the body; Calypso threatens the will to continue.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always interpret monsters SYMBOLICALLY — examiners want analysis, not just narrative Group the encounters by theme: temptation (Lotus-Eaters, Calypso, Sirens), violence (Cyclops, Laestrygonians), transformation (Circe) The Scylla and Charybdis episode is the best example of impossible moral choices Note how the encounters escalate in danger and decrease Odysseus's crew Link each monster to what it tests in Odysseus's character
